titleStmt.title: On the Benefits of Multicores for Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: On the Benefits of Multicores for Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In real-time and safety-critical systems, the move towards multicores is becoming unavoidable in order to keep pace with the increasing required processing power and to meet the high integration trend while maintaining a reasonable power consumption. However, the benefit expected from multicore platforms may not step up to the mark, and real-time constraints can be easily violated. Indeed, an efficient use of multicore platforms usually requires a suitable parallelization of the software and a proper knowledge of the hardware constraints in order to find the best trade-off between increasing the parallelization benefit and decreasing contentions from accessing shared resources. In this paper, we illustrate this duality and investigate a general approach to automate some deployment decisions in order to maximize the benefit from using multicores while meeting the schedulability constraints of the system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the last decade, a major technology fact was the adoption of multi-/manycore processors in order to benefit from the increasing technology scaling and to achieve high performance (embedded) computing systems with improved power efficiency. Industries have therefore moved towards multi-/manycore processors which provided a paradigm shift for modern software systems. These platforms previously restricted to the performance domain are currently being considered for safety critical domains such as avionics and automotive [1], [2], where there is a need for reducing the number of ECUs and providing more computational power for future applications.

However, one of the main challenges of multicores when applied to safety-critical systems is to manage the interference on shared resources [3], as multicores impose a strong timing correlation between shared hardware components. This same design factor which makes them very efficient in terms of performance makes them also very challenging in terms of predictability. Indeed, accesses to the shared resources in particular memory components, impose a strong timing dependency between concurrently running applications in the same chip. This introduces additional non-functional dependencies [4] which may induce unpredictable overload and therefore implies additional delays possibly violating the timing constraints of the system. Furthermore, standard commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) multicore components are optimized to improve the average case performance and not the worst case, caches behavior being the best example of such feature. This introduces a lot of non-determinism making the analysis of such systems very complex, if not unfeasible.

Therefore, interference on shared resources in multicores can seriously endanger the system safety when multiple concurrent accesses have to be considered. This effect is further worsened by the increase of the number of applications and cores integrated into the same system. Current products in the commercial processor landscape considered for safety-critical systems already feature hundreds of cores on a single chip [5].

The design of safety-critical real-time systems often makes use of formal methods and tools for timing analysis in order to prove the compliance of the system to the required timing constraints. Schedulability analysis [6], [7], is a well established method for analyzing existing industrial systems [8], such as in the automotive domain, to provide safe bounds on the response time of tasks sharing the same ECU or the same interconnect (e.g. Ethernet, XFDX, ... etc). An extensive area of research is currently how to extend these methods in order to analyze the effect of shared resources in multicore platforms. Several work, such as [9], [10], have provided response time analysis methods that specifically takes into account communication over the on-chip interconnect as well as an end-to-end analysis including both computation tasks and communication [11], [12].

In this paper, we present a detailed discussion about the duality between the parallelization benefit that can be achieved using multicore platforms and the overhead from accessing shared resources. This overhead depends on hardware factors such as the arbitration policy but also on the computation to communication ratio, characterizing differently each application. Therefore, we classify applications according to whether they are computation or communication intensive. Based on that, we extend existing timing analysis models in order to quantify both the parallelization benefits and shared resources overheads depending on the number of processors and some hardware and software parameters. The goal is to provide a general and high level methodology allowing the designer to automate at an early stage of the design some deployment decisions and to perform a rapid assessment of the parallelization potential of an application on a given multi-core target, in order to maximize the benefit from using multicores while meeting the timing constraints of the system.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows, Section II presents the considered system model and how we classify applications according to their computation to communication ratio. Section III shows how this factor influences the parallelization benefit and the overhead from shared resources. For that, we consider two parallelization strategies commonly used in multicores. Section IV discusses the importance of the deployment step and provides a schedulability test in order to exclude at design time unschedulable mapping solutions. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

div.head: A. Parallelization Gain and Overhead from Shared Resources
div.p: Multicore architectures are well established in generalpurpose computing and in application specific domains such as high performance computing, where it is well known that there is a tradeoff to find between the parallelization gain and the shared resources overhead.

With the use of multicore platforms, applications are expected to scale and perform better providing a performance factor which is proportional to the number of available processors. However, in practice and in the absence of a careful parallel design, applications may perform poorly on a multicore platform and provide poor scalability results. This is due to several factors, such as the parallelization capabilities of the software and the memory bottleneck which, despite the continuous technology improvement for building larger and faster memories, still remains the main bottleneck for performance in many hardware systems.

In real-time safety critical systems, these factors are even worsened by the re-use of a lot of legacy code which has been designed for the single core execution and by the use of many predictable mechanisms, such as the classical TDMA scheduling [13] for time and space isolation to allow a safe sharing of shared resources compliant with the certification constraints, but which often comes at the cost of low efficiency.

A comparison between a single core and a multicore execution of 3 tasks is illustrated in Figure 1. Applications have different execution times and the order of execution is determined by the cores's scheduling policy. As one can see, the single core execution is purely sequential and free from contentions on the shared resources1 , whereas the multicore execution is performed in parallel (every task is executed on a separate core) but suffers from the communication overhead resulting from the cores concurrent accesses to the shared resources. This will lead to a slow down of some tasks and a speedup of other tasks when executed on multiple cores, compared to the single core execution.

Note that, the overhead from shared resources is not identical for all tasks in the system, it is much larger for application C than application A and B. One major reason is that applications are not equal w.r.t their communication requirements. We therefore use this criteria in order to classify applications as computation and communication intensive tasks. We refer to app C as a communication intensive task. When running multiple applications in parallel using different cores, the overhead from shared resources is then much larger for communication intensive applications.

In the following, we provide for real-time tasks high level models for execution and response times, parametrized according to the above mentioned classification and considering some hardware parameters.

div.head: B. System Model
div.p: We assume standard periodic real-time tasks assigned a fixed static priority, and a multicore platform where every core implements a static priority preemptive (SPP) scheduler to arbitrate between tasks mapped on the same core/processor. Tasks mapped on different processors are executed in parallel and can therefore request shared resources concurrently.

Definition 1 (Task Model). We assume a set of n independent tasks {τ i , ..., τ n }. Each task τ i is characterized with the tuple (P i ; ρ i ; C i ; D i ) where, P i is the period of activation (or a minimum inter-arrival time), C i is the task execution time and D i is the deadline. Deadlines are assumed to be constrained, hence Di < P i. Tasks have a unique priority value ρ i thereby defining a global priority order. We use hp(i) (resp. lp(i)) to denote the set of tasks with higher (resp. lower) priority than task τ i .

Definition 2 (Platform Model). A multicore platform P is defined as P = {{p 1 , ..., p m }, δ}; where m is the number of processors, and δ : m -→ N is a scaling factor function characterizing the amount of communication overhead resulting from contentions on shared resources due to concurrent requests issued by other cores. We assume that this function is monotonically non decreasing as we increase the number of processors m. Note that this factor is hardware dependent and depends on multiple design choices, such as the structure of the memory hierarchy and the scheduling policy to arbitrate between requests on the shared resources (e.g. FIFO, TDMA). Definition 3 (Task Mapping). The mapping step links the software to the hardware. Given a number of n tasks and m processors (m << n) a mapping is a function μ : {τ 1 , ..., τ n } -→ {p 1 , ..., p m } with μ(τ i ) = p j means that the task τ i is mapped to processor p j .

div.head: 1) Task Execution Time:
div.p: In order to feature the computation to communication ratio characterizing each application, we decompose the task execution time C as follows,
div.formula: C = C omp + C om + C seq (1)
div.p: where, C omp is the time for performing computations and that can be parallelized, C om is the time for performing communication and C seq is the additional execution time that cannot be parallelizable.

2) Response Time Given a Single Processor: In the single processor case, the worst case response time, i.e the time between the activation of a task and its completion, accounting for the delay incurred from interfering tasks can be computed with the following iterative formula using the busy-window analysis, initially introduced in [14] and then elaborated in [7]. The algorithm builds on the critical instant according to which a task experiences its worst-case response time if it is activated simultaneously with all its interference and where all subsequent activations arrive as early as possible. The worst case response time R i of a task τ i under an SPP scheduler is defined as follows:
div.formula: R i = C i + j∈hp(i) R i P j .C j (2)
div.p: where, C i is the maximum execution time of task i when it runs in isolation. In a strictly periodic system, Ri Pj is the maximum amount of invocations of interfering tasks τ j during a time window of size R i . In SPP, interfering tasks correspond to higher priority tasks sharing the same processor and interrupting the execution of task i.

3) Upper Bound on the Response Time: Eq. 2 is a fixed point computation which can be calculated starting with R i = C i at the first iteration. In order to escape from the dynamics of the fixed point computation that can be performed using appropriate tools such as [15], we rely on the following continuous upper bound as proposed by [16].
div.formula: R up i = C i + j∈hp(i) C j 1 -j∈hp(i) U j(3)
div.p: where, U j = Cj Pj . This efficiently computable continuous upper bound on the response time can be easily derived as follows,
div.formula: R i = C i + Σ j∈hp(i) R i P j C j R i ≤ C i + Σ j∈hp(i) ( R i P j + 1) C j R i -R i (Σ j∈hp(i) U j ) ≤ C i + Σ j∈hp(i) C j R i ≤ C i + Σ j∈hp(i) C j 1 -Σ j∈hp(i) U j
div.p: Note that, tighter continuous upper bounds as proposed by [17] can also be considered.

div.head: 4) Schedulability Test:
div.p: A task set {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } is therefore schedulable if the response time for every task is smaller than its deadline, that is,
div.formula: ∀i R ub i = C i + j∈hp(i) C j 1 -j∈hp(i) U j ≤ D i (4)

div.head: III. PARALLELIZATION AND RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: In a multicore setting, both contentions on the shared resources and the parallelization strategy change the tasks execution and response times. We assume 2 parallelization strategies illustrated in Figure 2 and influencing differently the performance of the system: AMP (asymmetric mappings) and SMP (symmetric) [18], also known as task and data parallelism. AMP refers to the case where each application is mapped to a different core and SMP refers to the case where the same application is partitioned to be mapped to all available cores. Fig. 2: Different parallelization strategies for multicores.

In the following, we extend the formulations presented in the previous Section in order to take into account the parallelization factor and the number of processors. This is further implemented as part of the pyCPA tool [15] in order to evaluate the speedup of the worst case response time (WCRT) on tests sets generated using the UUniFast [19] algorithm.

div.head: A. Asymmetric Parallelization
div.p: As explained previously, contention on the shared resources increase as we increase the number of used processors, thereby increasing the time each task spends in communicating data. The execution time C i of a task i given m cores running concurrently becomes,
div.formula: C i (m) = C omp i + C om i • δ(m) + C seq i (5)
div.p: where, the communication load C om i is increased by the hardware overhead δ(m) of accessing shared resources.

The induced communication overhead is obviously larger for tasks exhibiting a high communication factor C om i . If this latter is small then the task execution time is less influenced by the shared resource/communication overhead as we increase the parallelization and therefore the number of processors.

Each mapping choice μ splits the set hp(i) of higher priority tasks than τ i into two complementary subsets, hp(i, p) (resp. hp(i, ¬p)) of high priority tasks mapped on the same (resp. different) processor p. Given multiple processors, the worst case response time of Eq 2 can be extended as follows to include the shared resources overhead and higher priority tasks mapped on the same processor,
div.formula: R i (m, μ) = C i (m) + j∈hp(i,p) R i (m, μ) P j .C j (m) (6)
div.p: Note that, the use of multiple cores/processing units allows to reduce the number of interfering tasks on the same processor, where higher priority tasks can be offloaded to be executed on other processors. Therefore, lower priority tasks can improve their timing as the preemption overhead resulting from higher priority tasks is reduced. This constitutes the parallelization benefit from the AMP parallelization strategy which increases as we increase the number of processors.

In the example depicted in Figure 3 ran using the pyCPA tool on a selected, we observe as we increase the number of processors a (super-linear) speedup of lower priority tasks (T1 Fig. 3: Speedup of the WCRT as we increase the number of processors using AMP. and T2) as higher priority tasks (i.e T3 and T4) are offloaded to other processors/cores. we observe on the other hand a slowdown of the response time of highest priority tasks as they do not get any benefit from the preemption gain and only suffer from the shared resources overhead, in particular if a task has a high communication factor. Note also that increasing the number of processors may not necessarily improve the overall system's response time because of the induced high shared resources overhead. In the provided example, for task T2 we observe a slowdown of the response time with the use of 4 processors compared to 2 processors. In this example, 2 processors seem to represent a good trade-off providing T1 with a large speedup and T3 and T4 with a moderate slowdown, compared to the single processor results.

div.head: B. Symmetric Parallelization
div.p: Symmetric mapping assumes that each application/task is mapped to all cores. This means that each task τ i is split into a set of sub-tasks with a reduced execution load. The task τ i is therefore accelerated by all sub-tasks executed in parallel on a different processor. However, similarly to AMP, this will result in a communication overhead from all processors accessing during execution shared resources to fetch the data required for computation. Therefore, the execution time C i of a task i given m cores running concurrently becomes,
div.formula: C i (m) = C omp i m + δ(m) * C om i + C seq i (7)
div.p: where, the computation load C omp i is divided by the number of used processors, and the communication load C om i is increased as previously by the hardware overhead δ(m) of accessing shared resources. the best trade-off which maximize the benefit of parallelization with a tolerable overhead due to shared resources, thereby minimizing for each task τ i the total execution time C i (m).
div.formula: m * i = C omp i δ * C om i (8
div.p: Note that, as we increase the number of processors, the execution time C i (m) may increase (after some value of m) to exceed the value C i (1) of the single processor case because of the dominant increase in the communication overhead. We refer to this point2 as mi which represents an upper bound on the number of "useful" processors. Indeed, it is clear that there is no point in using more processors than mi since the performance will be necessarily worse than the single processor case and where there is no parallelization benefit. Under SMP, every sub-task i mapped on a given core is interfering with all sub-tasks j ∈ hp(i) from higher priority tasks mapped on the same processor. Therefore, given m processors the worst case response time R i (m) of task i becomes,
div.formula: R i (m) = C i (m) + j∈hp(i) R i (m) P j • C j (m)(9)
div.p: As we increase the number of processors, the behavior of the tasks execution time influence the tasks response time. Figure 5 illustrates the behavior of the response time as we increase the number of processors combining the execution times of interfering tasks and their activation. Note that for each value of m, the same value is applied to all interfering tasks in addition to task i. In this example, we can clearly see that task τ i is communication intensive since it benefits slightly from the parallelization (i.e decrease in the execution time) as we increase the value of m. On the contrary, interfering tasks τ j ∈ hp(i) are computation intensive since they benefit from the parallelization. Overall, the behavior of the response time follows a similar trend than the execution time as we increase the number of processors. We refer to the response time execution as being in the computation regime when the parallelization gain is dominant and there is an increase in the speedup (i.e the response time is reduced) with the increase of the number of processors, and in the communication regime when the communication overhead is dominant and there is a slow down of the response time. The switch between the computation and communication regime is performed at a given value of m that can also be derived analytically.

The execution time plot follows the trend illustrated in Figure 4 where we also observe an increase in the communication overhead for tasks as we increase the number of processors to exceed (after some value of mi ) the values for the single processor case. This is the case for all tasks except τ 4 where we observe a decrease of the execution time as we increase the number of processors. This is due to the high computation factor of this task (ref. Table 1) compared to the communication factor, which therefore highly benefits from the parallelization as we increase the number of processors.

div.p: Figure 7 shows the evolution of the WCRT R i computed using the pyCPA tool for all tasks from the selected test case as we increase the number of processors. The evolution of the execution time when tasks run in isolation has obviously the same influence on the WCRT. This is observed in the WCRT plots (see, Figure 5) where we also observe an increase in the WCRT as we increase the number of processors to exceed after a given value of m the WCRT for the single processor case. It becomes clear that there is no point in increasing the degree of parallelism beyond this value as the overall WCRT results become worse than the single processor case. Note that, AMP and SMP strategies can be combined and the proposed formulations for the tasks execution and response times can be further extended to propose an additional formulation considering a combination of both parallelization strategies.

div.head: IV. DEPLOYMENT AND SCHEDULABILITY
div.p: The number of used processors has certainly an effect in determining the communication overhead however the deployment decision and the choice of tasks clustering has a crucial role in determining the parallelization benefit. Indeed, as discussed previously, the use of the maximum number of available processors/cores may not be beneficial because of the induced high communication overhead. Therefore, a wise clustering of tasks mapped on the same processor based on the tasks characteristics (computation to communication ratio and the combination of interfering tasks) can highly optimize the preemption overhead without highly increasing the communication overhead and therefore maximize the parallelization benefit when using multicores. clustering solutions for 4 tasks using 2 processors. One can observe that the two mapping solutions only differ with a task swap between T2 and T4. However one can also observe that this simple switch between 2 tasks can have a significant influence on the performance, for instance the speedup of task T2 jumps from a speedup factor of 1.33 in the first mapping solution to a speedup factor of 3.1 in the second mapping choice, given 2 processor. As discussed in Section III-A, higher priority tasks suffer in both cases of a slowdown of a factor of 0.68 due to the shared resources overhead proportional to the number of processors and to the task's communication factor C om . Figure 9 presents for the same setup the WCRT speedup of all tasks given an exhaustive exploration of all mapping solutions. In this case, we also observe a large variation between all combinations considering 2 processors.

In the following, we derive a schedulability condition, based on the continuous upper bound on the response time, that can be used to exclude mapping solutions that violate the deadline of some tasks and explore mapping solutions that optimize performance. Given a mapping μ and a number of processors m, we extend the bound on the response time defined in Eq. 3 for the single processor case as follows,
div.formula: R up i (m, μ) = C i (m) + j∈hp(i,p) C j (m) 1 -j∈hp(i,p) U j (m)(10)
div.p: where, U j (m) = Cj (m) Pj . In order to distinguish the factors characterizing the parallelization gain and the shared resources overhead, we use algebraic manipulations to obtain the following, We can similarly extend the schedulability test in Eq. 4 to obtain the following schedulability test,
div.formula: R up i (m, μ) = (C i + Σ j∈hp(i) C j ) + M O -I G (1 -Σ j∈hp(i) U j ) + U G -U O (11

div.p: where, M O , U O , U G and I G are the overhead and gain factors defined previously. α and β are the following constants,
div.formula: α = D i β = C i + Σ j∈hp(i) C j + Σ j∈hp(i) U j
div.p: We can clearly see from Eq. 12 that the schedulability test is satisfied for a given mapping μ and a number of processor m, when the parameters value of the parallelization gain are higher than the parameters value of the shared resources overhead.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: There is certainly a timing benefit from using multicores for real-time systems, However this benefit is conditioned by several factors, such as deployment decision, the overhead from shared resources and the number of used processors which is rapidly scaling. Therefore this benefit can only be achieved by finding appropriate trade-offs. For that, we need timing analysis tools in order to answer such complex questions and allow to capture the behavior of the system using models to exclude trial and error methods. In this paper, we presented high level models based on an abstract characterization of the software and hardware that can be used at design time in order to reason about deployment decisions and tasks distribution. This allows to exclude unschedulable mapping configurations and provide estimation about the expected performance of the system when using multicores.
